newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Transnet sees retrenchments widening loss.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Transnet sees retrenchments widening loss.

text.p: South African transport parastatal Transnet Ltd expects retrenchment costs to widen its 1997/98 accumulated losses over the previous year, its managing director Saki Macozoma said on Monday.
The retrenchment of some 3,500 exployees at PX, the group's ailing container and parcel delivery business, is expected to add more than 250 million rand to Transnet's 1997/98 costs.
But operational performances are seen improving.
"We think that next year will be a year where we take a knock on the bottom line but at the operating level we'll want to increase what we have," Macozoma told Reuters after a news conference.
He announced earlier that Transnet's accumulated loss for the year to March 31 had narrowed to 170 million rand from 253 million rand a year ago.
As for the 1995/96 year, massive pension fund deficit service costs -- 2.1 billion rand in total -- dragged the bottom line into the red.

Macozoma said the pensions hit would reduce this year as a result of the restructuring of health benefits and the phasing out of annual overpayments which have helped pare the liability to about 3.2 billion rand.
Pre-tax operating profits increased 4.6 percent to 3.04 billion rand, mainly on the back of a surge in profits at the company's rail unit, Spoornet.
Spoornet's net profit after finance costs jumped to 712 million rand from 98 million rand previously.

"The reason why that unit was able to achieve that result was that in the beginning of the last financial year we restructured Spoornet from a regional organisation which exhibited a number of feudal aspects into two focused components," Macozoma said.
The Spoornet contribution was largely offset by a slump at national flag carrier South African Airways (SAA), which dived 323 million rand into the red from a previous profit of 324 million rand.
Macozoma said SAA had been hit by poor cost management in particular. The cost of international crews, fuel and the weaker rand were key issues which he expected to be resolved over fiscal 1997/98.

"We see those as non-recurring items. They're not fundamental. With regard to fundamental issues, we think there is great room for improvement in yield management, load factors and other revenue enhancing programs," he said.
SAA also hoped to wring cost savings out of a revamp of its information technology systems.
He said the airline's losses were unlikely to grow but declined to speculate further on its likely 1997/98 financial results.
